Sometime in mid-late November

As Simone Peter looked up at the tall man who’s just entered her office, she realized that she’d made the terrible mistake of getting out of bed that morning.

On a good day, Simone Peter, co-leader of the Greens alongside Cem Özdemir, could expect hell. People needing her aide while Herr Özdemir was bust drumming up support. She would have meetings and people to see, constituents to talk with, and bills to help get through local Länder to improve the environment.

Today was not going to be a good day, and she wished for but a moment that she were an alcoholic.

The man closed the door behind him and smiled a winning smile that might have made a less experienced women drop her panties. But Simone was made of sterner things. And at age 62 with a birthday set for next month, she was no spring chicken.

“Steiner,” she said in a cool voice. She looked the man over. His blue eyes shone with a charm so powerful that they put her on edge. A part of her wondered for a moment if most of the DNVP were women. Girls did love bad boys, did they not?

How old was Steiner? Thirty-one, correct? Literally half her age. He was a pup with no business in politics, yet here the Nazi bastard was, pulling strings in the Bundestag. Now, he was in her office.

“How did you even get into my office?” she demanded.

He shrugged. “Well, I took a wrong turn, got sent on a quest to save a maiden from a dragon, sat around eating potato chips with her thereafter, then decided to pay a dear old friend a visit. Anything so wrong wit that?” he said in a matter-of-fact way.

“We’ve never met before, Steiner,” she replied, leaning back. “So, tell me why I shouldn’t call for police to escort you out of my office.”

“Because you’re such a nice lady?” Steiner asked, shooting her a hopeful smile.

She reached for her intercom. First, she was going to ask hr secretary to call the police. Then she was going to fire her secretary for letting Steiner in here.

The man took a hard step forwards. “Uh-uh-uh, Frau Peter, I think you will want to hear me out.”

Simone paused, her finger almost on the button. She raised an eyebrow.

“See, I got to talking with Herr Özdemir,” he said in a casually voice. “Nice guy, all things considered,. a bit too Turkish for my liking, but diverse world, we all gotta get along, y’know?”

The woman had to hold in a growl.

“Anyhow, so we got to agreeing that Rosenthal and his boys really did pull on over your eyes with the Volga German bill.”

“That was your work, fascist,” she all but spat.

Steiner frowned. For a moment, Simone wondered if she’s actually hurt his feeling, but then he spoke. “You’re so hurtful, Frau. All I want is the best for my nation and her people, same as you. My methods and way of seeing it through are all that differs between us. Hell, I even love the environment. Perhaps more so than you. I assure you, we thank you greatly for helping us get this bill over. And I’m rather upset they pulled money out of your precious child, so to speak, to fund my project.” He pounded a fist across his breast. “Hand aufs Herz, I had naught to do with that part. That was all the SPD’s idea.”

Simone set her hands down. “And?”

“And I’ll have you know the DNVP repays its favors. You did us a solid with the Volga German bill.”

“Why would I believe you?” she asked, leaning back in her chair. The leather creaked slightly. Her eyes darted away from his flicked over to the wall, whereupon her bookcase lay.

“What cause would I have to lie to you? You were there. do you recall DNVP members voting in favor of taking funds from your project? You will recall we voted against that.”

“Only because you wanted to take way more funds from it on behalf of your pet immigrant project,” she replied in a calm voice. Simone cross her hands and looked up at the man.

He shook his head. “Untrue. We wanted to take it away from money Rosenthal was funneling into refugee camps, not from the green energy project—a project, mind you, that neither Rosenthal nor Merkel cared to tap into once it was set up. Aside from a few dams in the Alps, of course. If my calculations are correct, with the 5 billion euros we’ve been putting into the fund without much cause, we will have 14.5 billion by the start of next year.”

She cocked a brow. “Do you not think I know about my ‘pet project’, as you called it.”

Steiner smiled again. His teeth looked white. She suddenly wondered if she’d remembered to brush her own teeth that morning. “Why, schöne Frau, I am here to see you over it.”

“Don’t hit on me, Steiner,” she warned, but her words seemed to run off him like rainwater off a steep roof.

“I had my boys do the math. Adding in all relative factors relating, it would cost about 5 million euros to build an industrial wind turbine. 14.5 billion dollars would allot for the construction of some 2900 wind turbines. That’s for them in total. This says nothing of afterward operating costs and the like. But think of all the energy Germany could produce like this!”

“What are you getting at, Steiner?”

“You know my talents, Frau Peter. I propose that as a way of sorry we’re sorry our plans hurt yours, we would lend all of you aid to helping push through a bill to use all of that money to create hundreds of new winds farms, countless jobs, and help Germany go greener.”

She leaned forwards. “Why would I bother working with you? you have 40 seats, I have 70.”

“Because I managed to get through a bill like the Volga German bill,” he told in a confident matter-of-fact way. “If I could get something like that to pass, we’d ve have trouble getting this across the board. And because if we don’t do it, you may lose your chance forever.”

“How?” she asked, narrowing her eyes.

“Because I have it on good authority that the trade bill that the SPD is trying to push in through with Russia will make their fossil fuels far easier to acquire than using windmills and other such energy plans.”

She just looked at him. “Bullshit.”

“Sure, don’t take my hearsay as anything but that,” he told her, nodding. “But do it at your own risk. I like you, Frau Peter. We’re very different, but we both stand for our beliefs. And right now, our shared belief in the environment may well be crippled because of corporate intent. Do you not see what I am trying to get at?”

After a moment, Simone nodded. “I do. And… I fear you may well be correct. Dammit, you’re a liar and a snake, but… for some reason, I don’t think you’re lying to me right this now.”

“So work with me,” he told her. “Allow us to help propose a bill to use that 14.5 billion dollars for something worth it while they’re still time.”

“Together, the Greens and the Nazis?” she scoffed, with a half-smile.

“Stranger things have happened,” he said with a shrug. “If you’d like, we can chat it over over a cup a coffee.”

She blinked. “Wait, are… are you asking me out?”

Steiner shot her a look of surprise. “Why, Frau Peter, I did think you thought of me that way! To think such an innocent request would be interpreted as a date—my!”

Simone felt herself reddening. “I-uh-I—”

“Well, if you want to fantasize, I won’t stop you. Coffee, then? I promises to be all business, but you can allow yourself to be as unprofessional as you will.” He winked.

Almost against herself, Simone Peter felt her head nodding.

[tl;dr Steiner and Simone Peter agree to work together to make use of an old fund to build wind turbines. They go out for coffee.]
